language_wrapper: Consider an alphabet of {alphabet_size} letters labeled 1,2,...,{alphabet_size} arranged in a cyclic order. A length-{word_length} word is called good if whenever the letter i appears, the next letter cannot be the letter numbered ((i + {step} - 1) mod {alphabet_size}) + 1 (with wrap-around into {1,...,{alphabet_size}}). Among all such good words, how many begin with letter {start_index}, end with letter {end_index}, and use every letter at least once?
hardness_rationale: The seed problem counts length-7 words over three letters with a simple adjacency restriction, solvable by a short recurrence or basic adjacency-matrix counting. Our family generalizes the alphabet size and introduces a forbidden cyclic successor offset, then imposes two global constraints: fixed start and end letters and the requirement that every letter appears at least once. Solving requires the transfer-matrix method together with inclusion–exclusion over all letter subsets that contain the start and end, i.e., evaluating (A_T)^{n-1} for many induced subgraphs T and summing with alternating signs. This blends graph walk enumeration, matrix exponentiation, and combinatorial sieving, significantly increasing difficulty and preventing solution by simple guesswork.
notes:
Problem family explanation: We consider a directed graph on m letters where each vertex i has all outgoing edges except to (i + d) mod m. Good words correspond to walks of length n-1 in this graph. The added constraints (fixed start and end; using all letters at least once) require counting only those walks that visit every vertex at least once.

Proof of correctness: Let U = {1,2,...,m} index the letters and A be the m×m adjacency matrix with A[i,j] = 1 if j ≠ (i + d) mod m and 0 otherwise (indices 0-based in computation). For any subset T ⊆ U containing s and e, let A_T be the adjacency matrix of the induced subgraph on T (obtained by restricting rows and columns to T). The number of good words of length n starting at s and ending at e that use only letters from T equals (A_T^{n-1})[s,e]. By inclusion–exclusion over forbidden letters, the number of good words that use every letter at least once equals ∑_{T ⊆ U, {s,e} ⊆ T} (-1)^{m - |T|} (A_T^{n-1})[s,e]. This is the standard principle: counting sequences avoiding any letter from U\T contributes with alternating signs, ensuring exactly those sequences that avoid none of the letters (i.e., include all letters) remain. Since walks are faithfully counted by powers of the adjacency matrix, the formula is exact.

Why this preserves the core idea: The seed’s constraint forbidding A→B, B→C, C→A is precisely the d=1 cyclic successor restriction on m=3 letters. Our generalization keeps the same adjacency logic but extends the alphabet and adds global visitation and boundary constraints, necessitating inclusion–exclusion with transfer matrices.

Implementation note: The verifier enforces domain constraints (3 ≤ m ≤ 10, m ≤ n ≤ 60, 1 ≤ d ≤ m−1, valid 1-based indices for s,e) and rejects trivial instances by ensuring the constrained count is strictly between 0 and the unconstrained walk count from s to e. Matrix exponentiation uses integer arithmetic and repeated squaring; inclusion–exclusion iterates over 2^{m−2} subsets containing s and e, which remains efficient for m ≤ 7 (and acceptable up to m ≈ 10 with the given bounds).
source_question: Define a $\text{good word}$ as a sequence of letters that consists only of the letters $A$ , $B$ , and $C$ - some of these letters may not appear in the sequence - and in which $A$ is never immediately followed by $B$ , $B$ is never immediately followed by $C$ , and $C$ is never immediately followed by $A$ . How many seven-letter good words are there?
